summary: Describes filters that limit location notifications in SIP to compelling events, so a subscriber is not flooded with every small change. They extend the event notification filtering format in RFC 4661 and build on the SIP presence package of RFC 3856. Locations use the existing PIDF-LO format.

eli5.summary: Instead of being told every time someone moves a step, you can ask to hear only when they leave the city. This lets SIP subscribers set such conditions for location updates.

questions: what is a sip location filter
how to filter sip location notifications
subtitle: Lets a SIP subscriber say when it wants location updates, so it is told about meaningful moves instead of every small change.

tldr.problem: Location changes continuously, so it is hard to know when a change is big enough to warrant a SIP notification, and subscribers risk being flooded with unimportant ones.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the XML event notification filter format of RFC 4661 with location-specific filters: distance moved, speed, civic value changes, entering or exiting a region, requested location type, and rate control.
tldr.outcome: A subscriber receives location notifications only when something it cares about happens, with the location carried in PIDF-LO over the SIP presence event package.

today: RFC 6447 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the event filter format of RFC 4661 and the rate control of RFC 6446.

sections.title: Why Location Needs Filters
sections.content:
SIP event notification (RFC 3265) lets a subscriber ask a notifier to send asynchronous updates, and the presence event package (RFC 3856) can carry location in the PIDF-LO format (RFC 4119). The hard part is deciding when to send a notification. Location can change along a continuous gradient, so it is difficult to know when a change is large enough to matter.

The subscriber should get notifications with appropriate frequency and granularity, without being flooded with ones that are not important to its application. RFC 6447 therefore extends the filter format of RFC 4661. A filter persists until it is replaced by a newer filter or until the subscription ends.
sections.eli5: If a friend's phone told you about every single step they took, you would stop paying attention. Filters let you say which news is worth hearing.

sections.title: What the Filters Can Trigger On
sections.content:
The RFC describes six cases in which a notification can be provided: the Target moves more than a specified distance since the last notification; the Target exceeds a specified speed; the Target enters or exits a 2-dimensional region, a circle or a polygon; civic location values change; the requested type of location information changes, for example from civic to geodetic; and a certain amount of time passes.

To keep the number of options down and reduce interoperability problems, implementations MUST support the <ns-bindings>, <filter> and <trigger> elements of RFC 4661, except for the <added> and <removed> sub-elements of <trigger>.
sections.eli5: You get a menu of reasons to be told: they moved far, they went fast, they crossed a fence, or enough time went by.

sections.title: Movement, Speed and Value Changes
sections.content:
The <moved> element holds a distance in meters. It is the minimum distance the resource must have moved since the last notification was sent, measured absolutely from the point of the last notification and including vertical movement. It MUST NOT appear more than once under a <filter>. The RFC's example uses 300.

Speed uses the <changed> element from RFC 4661 together with the <speed> element from RFC 5962, defined in meters per second. The condition can be met by a change on any axis, including altitude. The example fires when speed changes by 3 meters per second.

Changes in element values, such as civic address parts, also use <changed>. For example, a filter can fire when the country changes from FR to something else. Separate <trigger> elements fire when any one of several values changes, while several <changed> elements inside one trigger fire only when all of them change. Civic tokens such as country and A1 to A6 are hierarchical, so a change in A3 may also change A4, A5 and A6.

For both speed and value changes, an implementation MUST support <ns-bindings> to replace the namespace prefix, and the XPath expression MUST start with // followed by a single element. No other form of XPath is supported.
sections.eli5: You can say 'tell me when they have moved a football field away' or 'tell me when the street name changes', and you hear nothing until then.

sections.title: Entering or Exiting a Region
sections.content:
The <enterOrExit> condition is satisfied when the Target enters or exits a 2-dimensional region. The region is a polygon or a circle as defined in RFC 5491, and the element MUST contain one of them and MUST NOT contain more than one.

If the Target was outside, the notifier sends a notification when the Target is within the region with at least 50% confidence. If it started inside, the notifier notifies when the Target is outside with at least 50% confidence. Confidence inside plus confidence outside is limited by the confidence of the location itself, which is always less than 100%. The benefit is that small movements near the border, relative to the uncertainty of the location, do not trigger notifications.
sections.eli5: Imagine a fence drawn around a park. You hear about it only when your friend is pretty clearly in or out, not when they wobble along the fence line.

sections.title: Location Type and Rate Control
sections.content:
The optional <locationType> element, a child of <what>, lists the kinds of location the subscriber wants: any, geodetic or civic. If it is absent, any is assumed. With the exact attribute set to true, the notifier MUST return the requested type or no location at all. With false, the default, it MAY add other types or substitute one if the request cannot be met, and it SHOULD list civic and geodetic in the order requested.

For timing, the RFC uses two Event header field parameters from RFC 6446: min-rate and max-rate, which set a minimum and maximum notification rate per second. Only these two are required. When the time since the last notification exceeds the interval corresponding to 1 / min-rate, the current state is sent in its entirety, as after a subscription refresh.

A notifier must send a NOTIFY immediately after a subscription is created, and it may carry no content if state is not available yet. A later NOTIFY with location follows so the rate falls between the two limits. This matters, for example, in emergency call routing, where some location is needed within a short, pre-defined time even if it is uncertain.
sections.eli5: You can ask for the address as a street name or as map coordinates, and you can set a timer so you hear something at least every so often, but not too often.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC defines only filters and relies on other documents for security: SIP event notification (RFC 3265), the presence event package (RFC 3856), the filter framework (RFC 4661) and PIDF-LO (RFC 4119). It says security and privacy aspects are best covered by Section 9 of RFC 3856 and the GEOPRIV architecture in RFC 6280.

Authorization policies that limit access to location are provided by other protocols, such as Common Policy (RFC 4745). The geolocation policy format does not define specific policies for controlling filters. Because uploading filters strongly affects how a server handles a request, messages containing this extension must be authenticated and authorized, as RFC 4661 discusses.
sections.eli5: Telling the system what to watch for is powerful, so it must check who is asking and whether they are allowed to know.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers an XML namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:location-filter, and an XML schema, urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:location-filter. The schema itself appears as the sole content of Section 4 of the RFC. The registrant contact is the IETF GEOPRIV Working Group, as delegated by the IESG.
sections.eli5: The new filter names are written in an official list so nobody else uses the same ones.

messages.label: SUBSCRIBE (1)
messages.note: Creates the subscription with filters and large min-rate and max-rate values.

messages.label: NOTIFY (3)
messages.note: Full state, between min-rate and max-rate.

items.label: Distance moved
items.desc: Meters since the last notification, including vertical movement.

items.label: Value or speed change
items.desc: RFC 4661 element, used with //speed or civic address tokens.

items.label: Region crossing
items.desc: A circle or polygon, at least 50% confidence.

items.label: Location type
items.desc: any, geodetic or civic, with an optional exact attribute.
